title: Advances in AI-designed base editors pave the way for next-generation gene therapy
excerpt: A joint research team led by Daesik Kim, a professor in the Department of Medicine at Sungkyunkwan University, along with Yong-Sub Kim, a professor at the University of Ulsan College of Medicine, and Jae-Hyun Park, a professor at Sungkyunkwan University School of Medicine, has developed "OpenABE" (Open Adenine Base Editor).
content_html:
A joint research team led by Daesik Kim, a professor in the Department of Medicine at Sungkyunkwan University, along with Yong-Sub Kim, a professor at the University of Ulsan College of Medicine, and Jae-Hyun Park, a professor at Sungkyunkwan University School of Medicine, has developed "OpenABE" (Open Adenine Base Editor).

By precisely engineering AI-derived next-generation base editors using structure-guided protein engineering, the team increased gene-editing efficiency by up to 36-fold compared with conventional models. This research laid a foundation for safely treating various previously intractable genetic diseases.

The findings were published in the journal Nucleic Acids Research.

Early AI editors fell short

Adenine base editors (ABEs), a key gene-editing technology, locate incorrect letters (adenine) and correct them into proper letters (guanine) within the DNA sequence—the blueprint of life.

Recently, research using artificial intelligence to rapidly design novel gene editors not found in nature has drawn significant attention in the scientific community. However, initial models created by AI suffered from low gene-editing efficiency and frequent off-target and bystander effects, in which unintended genetic letters outside the target site were altered, limiting their safety for clinical applications in patients.

Structural tweaks boosted performance

Through AlphaFold-based predictions, Kim's joint research team analyzed the three-dimensional structure of base editors as if examining a 3D map. Through this analysis, they identified critical regions that help the editor firmly grasp the target DNA without losing its hold.

The team conducted precise structural engineering by introducing customized mutations to these key regions and appending a specialized tail structure derived from the top-performing conventional base editor.

The resulting next-generation gene editors, "OpenABE 1.1" and "OpenABE 1.2," demonstrated editing capabilities 16 to 36 times greater than existing AI-designed gene editors. This performance puts them on par with ABE8e, currently considered the gold-standard gene editor used in laboratories worldwide.

Furthermore, the team dramatically reduced off-target effects surrounding target genes—a chronic issue in AI gene editors—achieving high precision that corrects only the intended genes.

Beyond the cell nucleus

Notably, this study showed that precise editing is achievable not only for DNA inside the nucleus—the center of the cell—but also for DNA within mitochondria, which produce cellular energy but have proven difficult to edit because of their unique structure.

Additionally, by encapsulating these gene editors into engineered virus-like particles (eVLPs) for cellular delivery, the team achieved high safety standards that allow the selective editing of only one or two target genes needing treatment.

Kim stated, "This study represents a landmark innovation where human scientists overcame the limitations of early AI-designed gene editors using structure-guided protein engineering. By opening a path to safely cure the causes of genetic diseases in both the nucleus and mitochondria, we expect this work to significantly accelerate the development of therapeutics for genetic disorders."

Broader gene-editing platform

The research team also recently revealed that "OpenCRISPR-1," a next-generation gene editor designed by AI, maintains gene-editing efficiency comparable to conventional Cas9 while reducing off-target mutations by up to 553-fold.

Furthermore, by applying OpenCRISPR-1 to prime editing technology and engineered virus-like particle (eVLP) delivery systems, they demonstrated its potential for expansion into a highly efficient and precise next-generation gene therapy platform.

Publication details

Hye-Yeon Hwang et al, Structure-guided engineering of AI-derived adenine base editors for nuclear and mitochondrial DNA editing, Nucleic Acids Research (2026). DOI: 10.1093/nar/gkag737

content_html_zh:
由成均馆大学医学系教授 Daesik Kim、蔚山大学医学院教授 Yong-Sub Kim 和成均馆大学医学院教授 Jae-Hyun Park 领导的联合研究小组开发了“OpenABE”（开放腺嘌呤碱基编辑器）。

通过使用结构引导的蛋白质工程精确设计人工智能衍生的下一代碱基编辑器，该团队将基因编辑效率比传统模型提高了 36 倍。 这项研究为安全治疗各种以前难以治愈的遗传疾病奠定了基础。

研究结果发表在《核酸研究》杂志上。

早期的人工智能编辑功亏一篑

腺嘌呤碱基编辑器 (ABE) 是一项关键的基因编辑技术，可在 DNA 序列（生命的蓝图）中定位不正确的字母（腺嘌呤）并将其纠正为正确的字母（鸟嘌呤）。

最近，利用人工智能快速设计自然界中未发现的新型基因编辑器的研究引起了科学界的高度关注。 然而，人工智能创建的初始模型存在基因编辑效率低、脱靶效应和旁观者效应频繁等问题，即目标位点之外的非预期遗传字母被改变，限制了其在患者临床应用的安全性。

结构调整提升绩效

通过基于 AlphaFold 的预测，Kim 的联合研究小组分析了碱基编辑器的三维结构，就像检查 3D 地图一样。 通过这种分析，他们确定了帮助编辑牢牢抓住目标 DNA 而不会失去控制的关键区域。

该团队通过向这些关键区域引入定制突变并附加源自高性能传统碱基编辑器的专门尾部结构，进行了精确的结构工程。

由此产生的下一代基因编辑器“OpenABE 1.1”和“OpenABE 1.2”的编辑能力比现有人工智能设计的基因编辑器高出 16 至 36 倍。 这种性能使它们与 ABE8e 相当，ABE8e 目前被认为是全球实验室使用的黄金标准基因编辑器。

此外，该团队还大大减少了围绕目标基因的脱靶效应（人工智能基因编辑器中的一个长期问题），实现了仅纠正预期基因的高精度。

超越细胞核

值得注意的是，这项研究表明，精确编辑不仅适用于细胞核（细胞中心）内的 DNA，也适用于线粒体内的 DNA，线粒体产生细胞能量，但由于其独特的结构而被证明难以编辑。

此外，通过将这些基因编辑器封装到用于细胞传递的工程病毒样颗粒（eVLP）中，该团队实现了高安全标准，允许仅选择性编辑一两个需要治疗的目标基因。

Kim 表示：“这项研究代表了一项里程碑式的创新，人类科学家利用结构引导的蛋白质工程克服了早期人工智能设计的基因编辑器的局限性。 通过开辟一条安全治愈细胞核和线粒体遗传性疾病病因的途径，我们预计这项工作将显着加速遗传性疾病疗法的开发。”

更广泛的基因编辑平台

研究团队最近还透露，由AI设计的新一代基因编辑器“OpenCRISPR-1”，在保持与传统Cas9相当的基因编辑效率的同时，将脱靶突变减少高达553倍。

此外，通过将 OpenCRISPR-1 应用于引物编辑技术和工程病毒样颗粒 (eVLP) 递送系统，他们展示了其扩展为高效、精确的下一代基因治疗平台的潜力。
